messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rafael is a 51-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has been married for many years and works as a tax inspector, a job that requires him to sit for long stretches, move between offices, and enter unfamiliar buildings where he cannot always predict who will be in the room or how a conversation will unfold. He came to therapy after months of feeling increasingly on guard in ordinary settings and after noticing that his reactions were becoming difficult to explain to his wife and colleagues. The index trauma he described was a period of physical abuse by a romantic partner earlier in his adult life, a relationship he had trusted enough to let shape the rhythm of his days. He spoke of one particular evening when an argument turned physical without warning, leaving him with the sense that the person beside him could shift from familiar to dangerous in an instant. Even now, the most distressing aspect for Rafael was not only what happened, but that it happened at the hands of someone he had believed he could rely on. He said plainly that he felt betrayed by someone he trusted, and that this betrayal had altered how he understood other people’s intentions.

In the years since, fragments of that time have continued to intrude on him in ways he cannot control. He described sudden pieces of the memory appearing without warning and then disappearing, as if the event were broken into shards rather than one continuous scene. Sometimes a fragment would come while he was standing at a copier at work or waiting in line at a bank: a flash of a body moving too close, a surge of physical dread, and then the image would be gone before he could hold it. At other times the memory forced its way into his mind when he did not want it to, particularly when he was already tired and less able to keep his mind on the present. He also described parts of the event that he simply cannot remember no matter how hard he tries, which leaves him frustrated and unsettled, as though he has lost pieces of his own history but is still expected to live with it. He does not speak about these moments casually; he lowers his voice, looks away, and seems embarrassed by how little control he has over when they appear.

Rafael has become especially alert to sensations and situations that leave him feeling vulnerable. He is highly uneasy when he is very tired or exhausted, noticing that fatigue makes the world feel less manageable and less safe. On such days he is more likely to scan the environment and feel that something may go wrong without warning. He also notices discomfort in cramped or awkward settings, such as crowded meeting rooms or waiting areas where he cannot settle himself. Unpredictable situations are particularly difficult for him: an unexpected schedule change at work, a last-minute request from a supervisor, or being asked to step into an unfamiliar office can all leave him tense and braced. He said he does not like not knowing who might enter a room or what may happen next, because unpredictability now feels linked, in his mind, to danger.

These feelings have shaped how he moves through everyday life. At work, he prefers to position himself with his back against a wall when possible so he can see the room, and he often notices himself looking behind him to check whether someone is following him when walking through parking lots, hallways, or quiet streets after leaving an office visit. He is aware that these reactions may seem excessive, yet in the moment he experiences them as necessary precautions. He often reacts as if he is in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, and he is startled by how quickly his body moves into alarm. Over time this has made him more rigid in social and occupational settings. He sits through meetings with obvious tension, chooses seats carefully in restaurants with his wife, and has become reluctant to linger in places where he cannot easily see what is happening around him.

Rafael’s view of himself has also changed. He spoke of feeling like an object, not like a person, and he said this with a quiet sort of shame, as though the words were difficult to admit even in therapy. He has come to believe that nothing good can happen to him anymore, a conviction that has left him cautious about hope and doubtful about relief. Although he continues to function and has remained committed to his job and marriage, he described a bleak sense that future experiences may only repeat the same vulnerability. His wife has noticed that he is more guarded and that he often seems distant during family time, especially when he is fatigued or when plans change unexpectedly. What brought him to seek help now was the growing strain of living in this state of alertness and the fear that he may no longer be able to hide how much energy it takes to remain composed. He is most afraid that he will stay trapped in this sense of being unsafe and diminished, and most hoping that therapy might help him feel like himself again without having to brace for harm in every room.
